title: Circles
short: Tangents to a circle and the number of tangents from a point.
lede: Two theorems and a handful of standard figures cover this chapter.
lens: The rest of the **15-mark Geometry unit**, roughly **5–6 marks**.
Expect a tangent-length proof (3 marks) and objective questions on the number of tangents from a point.
concepts: **1. Tangent.** A line that touches the circle at exactly one point. That point is the **point of contact**.
**2. Theorem 10.1.** The tangent at any point of a circle is **perpendicular** to the radius through the point of contact.
**3. Theorem 10.2.** The lengths of tangents drawn from an **external point** to a circle are **equal**.

**4. Standard consequences.** A tangent is parallel to the tangent at the opposite end of a diameter; a parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus; and the angle between two tangents from an external point is supplementary to the angle subtended by the chord of contact at the centre.
formulas: Tangent ⊥ radius at the point of contact
PA = PB for tangents from an external point P
Tangent length = √(d² − r²), where d is the distance from the centre
tricks: - **Always join the centre to the point of contact.** That creates the right angle you need, and it is the first line of almost every proof here.
- For a triangle circumscribing a circle, let the tangent segments from each vertex be x, y, z. The three side lengths give three equations, and the perimeter is 2(x + y + z).
- “Prove the tangents are equal” is done by joining the centre to both points of contact and to the external point, then using RHS congruence.
- The angle between two tangents and the angle at the centre **add to 180°**.
mistakes: - Forgetting to state that the radius is perpendicular to the tangent — that is a marked step.
- Assuming the two tangent lengths are equal when the point is inside or on the circle.
- In the circumscribed-triangle problem, mixing up which segment belongs to which vertex.
- Writing “the angle is 90°” without naming the theorem that gives it.

qa.q: How many tangents can be drawn from a point inside a circle?
qa.a: None. A line through an interior point must cut the circle at two points.

qa.q: From a point 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, a tangent is drawn. Find its length.
a: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so the three lengths form a right triangle.

qa.q: Prove that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
a: Let P be the external point and PA, PB the tangents with points of contact A and B.
In ΔOAP and ΔOBP: OA = OB (radii), OP is common, and ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° (tangent ⊥ radius).
By RHS congruence, ΔOAP ≅ ΔOBP, so PA = PB.

qa.q: A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle. Prove that AB + CD = AD + BC.
a: Let the tangent segments from A, B, C, D be p, q, r, s respectively.
Then AB = p + q, BC = q + r, CD = r + s and AD = p + s.
AB + CD = p + q + r + s and AD + BC = p + s + q + r.
The two sums are identical, so AB + CD = AD + BC.

mcq.q: The number of tangents from a point on the circle is: (a) 0  (b) 1  (c) 2  (d) infinite
The angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact is: (a) 45°  (b) 60°  (c) 90°  (d) 180°
Two tangents from an external point to a circle are: (a) unequal  (b) equal  (c) always perpendicular  (d) parallel

trend: One tangent-length proof or numerical (3 marks) and objective questions on the number of tangents.
onepager: - Tangent ⊥ radius at the point of contact.
- Tangents from one external point are equal.
task: Draw a circle, take an external point, and construct both tangents with compass and ruler. Measure them — they should match, which is Theorem 10.2 in your hand.

title: Areas Related to Circles
lede: Perimeter of a sector and area of a segment — two formulas and a lot of care with the radius.
lens: Part of the **10-mark Mensuration unit**, roughly **4–5 marks**.
Typically one question on the perimeter or area of a sector, and one on a segment or a combined figure.
Only sectors and segments of a circle remain in the rationalised syllabus.
concepts: **1. Sector.** The region between two radii and the arc joining their endpoints. The angle at the centre is θ.
**2. Segment.** The region between a chord and the arc it cuts off. The minor segment uses the minor arc.

head: Quantity
Formula (θ in degrees)
rows: Area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord
Area of sector − area of that triangle

concepts: **3. Combined figures.** Most questions are a square or rectangle with quadrant-shaped corners removed, or a circle inscribed in a square. Subtract the parts you do not want.
**4. Circle inscribed in a square:** the diameter equals the side. **Circle circumscribing a square:** the diameter equals the diagonal, `a√2`.
formulas: Segment area = sector area − ½ r² sin θ
Perimeter of a sector = 2r + arc length
tricks: - **Perimeter of a sector is 2r + arc**, not just the arc. Missing the two radii is the most common error here.
- For θ = 90° the sector area is exactly one quarter of πr²; for θ = 60°, one sixth.
- Circle inscribed in a square of side a: wasted area = a² − πa²/4. Circle circumscribing it: wasted area = πa²/2 − a².
- Take π as 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7 — the arithmetic collapses. Otherwise use 3.14.
mistakes: - Forgetting to add the two radii to the perimeter of a sector.
- Using the diameter where the formula needs the radius.
- Computing the segment as sector minus chord *length* instead of sector minus **triangle area**.
- Mixing degrees and radians. The CBSE formulas use degrees only.

qa.q: Find the length of an arc of a sector with radius 21 cm and central angle 120°.
Find the area of a sector of radius 6 cm with a central angle of 60° (take π = 3.14).
Find the perimeter of a sector with radius 14 cm and central angle 90°.
A square of side 14 cm has a circle inscribed in it. Find the area between the square and the circle.
a: The inscribed circle has diameter 14 cm, so radius 7 cm.
Area of square = 196 cm². Area of circle = (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm².

mcq.q: The area of a quadrant of a circle of radius r is: (a) πr²/2  (b) πr²/4  (c) 2πr  (d) πr²
The perimeter of a sector includes: (a) only the arc  (b) the arc and one radius  (c) the arc and two radii  (d) the chord and the arc
The area of a segment is found by: (a) sector − triangle  (b) sector + triangle  (c) circle − sector  (d) triangle − sector

trend: One sector perimeter/area question and one combined-figure question. Quadrant corners cut from a square is the classic combined figure.
onepager: - Inscribed circle: diameter = side of square.
task: Cut four identical quadrants from the corners of a square card and lay them together — they form exactly one full circle when the radius is half the side.

title: Surface Areas and Volumes
short: Combinations of solids, conversion of solids, and the frustum.
lede: A table of formulas plus three standard question types. The frustum is worth learning separately.
lens: The rest of the **10-mark Mensuration unit**, roughly **5–6 marks**.
Expect one question on a combination of solids (3–4 marks) and one on conversion of solids or a frustum (3–4 marks).
Surface area questions almost always involve **removing** a surface where two solids join — that is where the marks are.
concepts: **1. Combinations of solids.** A solid made of two or more basic solids. Total surface area = sum of the *curved/lateral* surface areas actually exposed. Where two solids join, the joining face is **not** part of the outer surface.
**2. Volume is additive.** Unlike surface area, the volume of a combination is simply the sum of the volumes of its parts.
**3. Conversion of solids.** When one solid is melted and recast into another, or many small solids are combined into one, **the volume stays the same**. Set volume before = volume after and solve.
**4. Frustum of a cone.** The part of a cone left after a smaller cone is cut off the top by a plane parallel to the base. Its slant height is `l = √[h² + (R − r)²]`.

**5. Cylindrical hole drilled through a solid.** Subtract the cylinder’s volume, but its curved surface is now **exposed**, so add it to the surface area. Then remove the two circular faces where it was drilled.
formulas: Cone: CSA = πrl,  V = πr²h/3,  l = √(r² + h²)
Frustum: l = √[h² + (R − r)²],  CSA = π(R + r)l
Total surface area of a frustum = π(R + r)l + πR² + πr²
steps: 1. Sketch the solid and label every dimension, including any that must be inferred (for example the height of a cone placed on a cylinder).
2. Decide what is **exposed**. Cross out joining faces on the sketch.
3. Write the formula for each part separately before substituting anything.
4. For conversion problems, write *volume before = volume after* first, then substitute.
5. Give the final answer with units, and to the number of decimal places asked (usually two, with π = 22/7 or 3.14 as specified).
tricks: - **Hemisphere on top of a cuboid or cylinder:** the flat circular base of the hemisphere is *not* part of the outer surface. Use only its curved area, 2πr².
- **Cone on top of a cylinder with the same radius:** the joining circular face disappears from the surface area, but both heights add in the volume.
- **Conversion problems are one equation.** Number of small spheres × volume of one = volume of the big one. Do not compute individual volumes first.
- **Frustum slant height uses (R − r), not (R + r).** That single sign decides the whole answer.
- When a question says “slant height” is given, do not recompute it from r and h.
mistakes: - Including the joining face in the total surface area.
- Using πr²h for a cone instead of πr²h/3.
- Forgetting to divide by 3 for cones and pyramids.
- In conversion problems, equating *surface areas* instead of volumes. Melting preserves volume, never surface area.
- Writing the answer without units, or with the wrong unit (cm² for area, cm³ for volume).

qa.q: A solid consists of a cylinder with a hemisphere on one end and a cone on the other, all of radius 7 cm. The cylinder is 20 cm high, the cone 12 cm high. Find the total surface area (take π = 22/7).
a: Cone slant height l = √(7² + 12²) = √193 ≈ 13.89 cm, so cone CSA = (22/7) × 7 × 13.89 ≈ 305.6 cm².
Total ≈ 880 + 308 + 305.6 = 1493.6 cm². The two circular joining faces are not counted.

qa.q: A solid metallic sphere of radius 4.2 cm is melted and recast into a cylinder of radius 6 cm. Find the height of the cylinder.
a: Volume of sphere = volume of cylinder.

qa.q: 100 solid iron spheres, each of radius 1 cm, are melted to form one solid sphere. Find its radius.
A frustum of a cone has radii 14 cm and 7 cm and height 24 cm. Find its slant height and curved surface area (take π = 22/7).

mcq.q: The volume of a cone of radius r and height h is: (a) πr²h  (b) πr²h/3  (c) 2πr²h  (d) πrh
When a solid is melted and recast into another shape, which quantity is conserved? (a) surface area  (b) volume  (c) both  (d) neither
mcq.a: **(b) Volume.** Surface area almost always changes.

mcq.q: The slant height of a frustum with radii R and r and height h is: (a) √[h² + (R + r)²]  (b) √[h² + (R − r)²]  (c) h + R + r  (d) √(R² − r²)

trend: One combination-of-solids surface area question and one conversion or frustum question appear most years. The frustum has been asked repeatedly since it was retained in the syllabus.
onepager: - Surface area: count only what is exposed. Volume: always additive.
- Melting conserves volume, never surface area.
- Cone volume has the 1/3. Hemisphere CSA is 2πr², TSA is 3πr².
task: Take a cylindrical container and a cone of the same radius and height. Fill the cone with water and pour it into the cylinder three times — it should exactly fill it. That is the 1/3 in the cone formula.
